question: Can layer semantics determine norms and duality maps that compose recursively into architecture-aware steepest-descent directions, thereby unifying width-scalable parameterization and fast matrix-preconditioned optimization?

key_findings.claim: Modular dualization gives a clean recursive construction of a norm-steepest direction for a network assembled from typed modules.
key_findings.evidence: Each atomic module is assigned input/output norms, a weight norm, sensitivity, and mass so it is locally Lipschitz. Composition and concatenation induce a weighted-max modular norm; because the dual of a max-style product norm separates, Equations 11-12 recursively rescale and concatenate the atomic duality-map outputs.

key_findings.claim: For dense matrices, the proposed direction is a dimension-rescaled polar factor of the gradient; embeddings and convolutions receive different rules because their inputs have different semantics.
key_findings.evidence: A Linear gradient G=U Sigma V^T maps to sqrt(d_out/d_in) UV^T under the RMS-to-RMS operator norm. Embed instead normalizes every column in RMS under an l1-to-RMS norm. Conv2D splits the kernel into k^2 channel matrices and polarizes each with an additional 1/k^2 factor. This is a concrete argument against applying one coordinatewise optimizer rule to every tensor.

key_findings.claim: The claimed unification with muP and Shampoo is insightful but partial, not an equivalence of full optimizers.
key_findings.evidence: The Linear map recovers muP's width factor and a no-accumulation Shampoo-like UV^T direction. It does not recover muP's full parameterization across initialization/readout/learning rates, nor Shampoo's accumulated Kronecker second moments, damping, grafting, and update schedule. The paper itself calls these 'essential features' and 'partial approximations.'

key_findings.claim: Rectangular Newton-Schulz makes approximate polar updates GPU-friendly without an SVD, but finite-step accuracy, scaling, and end-to-end cost are not evaluated here.
key_findings.evidence: After spectral- or Frobenius-normalizing G, the cubic X_{t+1}=1.5X_t-0.5X_tX_t^TX_t pushes each nonzero singular value toward one; higher odd polynomials are suggested. The text discusses sketching and inverse roots qualitatively, but reports no error curves, iteration counts, precision tests, throughput, memory, communication, or optimizer benchmark.

key_findings.claim: This paper supplies a geometry and direction oracle rather than a complete, experimentally supported training algorithm for general networks.
key_findings.evidence: Steepest descent in Proposition 1 also needs the dual norm and a sharpness or step-size scalar; practical momentum, state accumulation, weight decay, parameter exclusions, distributed execution, and mass selection are unspecified. Atomic maps cover Linear, Embed, and a conservative Conv2D construction, while attention, normalization gains, biases, MoE routers, and recurrent/shared parameters are not instantiated. The only speed evidence is an external NanoGPT record attributed to a variant communicated via a workshop paper.

method.core_idea: Treat gradients as dual objects and map them into parameter updates using the norm geometry implied by each layer's input-output semantics and the network's composition graph.
method.mechanism: Choose atomic operator norms, solve their unit-norm linear maximization maps, recursively propagate sensitivity and mass factors through module composition/concatenation, and approximate matrix polar factors with a few GPU-efficient Newton-Schulz polynomial iterations.
assumptions: Chosen activation and operator norms approximate the anisotropic smoothness relevant to training.
Atomic modules satisfy the stated well-normed Lipschitz bounds near the current weights and activations.
Weighted-max composition captures the useful geometry of the full parameter space.
Module masses and sensitivities can be specified robustly for real architectures.
Approximate polar directions remain beneficial after momentum, stochastic noise, finite precision, and distributed execution.

techniques.role: Assigns different geometries to dense, embedding, and convolutional layers.
Recursively combines layer norms using mass and downstream sensitivity.
Selects the unit-norm update maximizing inner product with the gradient.
Equalizes nonzero singular values of matrix update directions.
Approximates the polar factor through matrix multiplications suited to accelerators.

evaluations.setting: Analytic Linear, Embed, and Conv2D modules
evaluations.metric: closed-form induced norm and duality map
evaluations.result: derives polar-factor, column-normalization, and per-kernel-slice polar maps
evaluations.baseline: raw Euclidean gradient and prior spectral-duality constructions

evaluations.metric: exact duality map of the induced weighted-max norm
evaluations.result: atomic maps combine recursively with explicit mass/sensitivity factors
evaluations.baseline: prior weighted-sum duality that updates only one layer

evaluations.result: normalized Newton-Schulz iterates converge to UV^T for nonzero singular directions
evaluations.baseline: exact SVD, randomized sketching, and inverse matrix-root iterations

evaluations.result: an external NanoGPT speedrun using a variant is cited, with no controlled experiment included
evaluations.baseline: no in-paper AdamW, Shampoo, or muP benchmark

limitations: No training experiments, ablations, timing, memory, or numerical-accuracy results appear in the paper.
It specifies update directions but not a complete optimizer or principled adaptive step-size rule.
Layer norms, masses, sensitivities, and atomic boundaries require human semantic choices.
Only three parameterized atomic layer types receive explicit maps.
The Conv2D per-slice max norm is a conservative bound, not the exact convolution operator norm.
The fast polar method is analyzed only asymptotically, without stochastic or finite-precision guarantees.
The rhetoric that gradient subtraction fails a type check depends on refusing the usual Euclidean Riesz identification; it is a design lens rather than a coordinate-free impossibility.
failure_modes: Poor module masses can over-update one branch or suppress feature learning in another.
Polarization amplifies tiny noisy singular directions to unit magnitude unless finite iterations, momentum, or regularization suppress them.
Rank-deficient minibatch gradients leave null directions untouched and can make behavior batch-size dependent.
Frequent Newton-Schulz matrix multiplications can erase sample-efficiency gains through wall-clock or communication overhead.
Treating a convolution as independent kernel slices can ignore spatial Fourier structure and weight sharing.
Unsupported layer types can force arbitrary fallback geometry, breaking architecture-wide scaling claims.
reusable_insights: Choose optimization geometry at the layer-semantic level rather than only by tensor shape.
Represent optimizers as compositional linear minimization oracles so architecture changes induce update rules mechanically.
Separate direction geometry, scalar step size, momentum, and regularization when comparing optimizer mechanisms.
Approximate matrix functions with accelerator-friendly polynomials when exact decompositions dominate runtime.
Benchmark both training FLOPs and elapsed time because matrix-aware updates trade extra compute for fewer tokens or steps.
open_questions: Which module norm best predicts local loss curvature rather than merely activation scale?
Can masses and sensitivities be inferred online with stable learning-rate transfer?
How should attention, normalization, shared weights, MoE, state-space layers, and biases be typed?
What finite-step Newton-Schulz accuracy is optimal under bf16/fp8 and distributed sharding?
When does polarizing small singular directions help feature learning versus amplify gradient noise?
Can one prove end-to-end convergence and width/depth transfer for the actual momentum-and-weight-decay optimizer now called Muon?

competitive_landscape.title: Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm
competitive_landscape.difference: Large et al. recursively define the norm, smoothness bounds, and update normalization for learning-rate transfer; Modular Duality derives the exact steepest-direction map of that norm and fast polar implementations.

competitive_landscape.title: Shampoo: Preconditioned Stochastic Tensor Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Shampoo accumulates Kronecker-factored second moments and inverse roots for adaptive preconditioning; the modular Linear map uses an instantaneous polar direction and interprets its no-accumulation form as one part of Shampoo.

competitive_landscape.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Muon operationalizes matrix orthogonalization with momentum, weight decay, update-scale rules, distributed implementation, scaling laws, and a 5.7T-token MoE run; Modular Duality provides the earlier compositional norm rationale but no such empirical validation.

competitive_landscape.title: Muon Optimizes Under Spectral Norm Constraints
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. place practical Muon in the Lion-K family and show decoupled weight decay implies spectral-norm-constrained optimization; Modular Duality derives the same polar direction as steepest descent under RMS operator norms and extends it compositionally to layer types.

competitive_landscape.title: Convergence of Muon with Newton-Schulz
competitive_landscape.difference: Kim and Oh prove stationary-point convergence for the actual finite-q Newton-Schulz approximation and quantify doubly exponential approach to exact polar behavior; Modular Duality only gives the asymptotic singular-value argument and suggests polynomial tuning.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A recursive architecture-level duality map unifies fast Shampoo-like and scalable muP-like training, with GPU-friendly maps for the layers needed by transformers and CNNs.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper gives explicit norm-dual derivations, composition rules, three atomic layer maps, and Newton-Schulz/sketching/inverse-root computation routes, while citing an external NanoGPT record.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The compositional type-and-norm framework is conceptually original and directly anticipated the influential Muon optimizer. At publication, however, it was a direction-design paper rather than evidence that the resulting optimizer was fast, scalable, or general; those claims gained substantial support only from subsequent large-scale Muon experiments and theory.

reviewer_notes: Read all 12 pages including every derivation and reference. The landscape was updated through primary arXiv/OpenReview records on 2026-08-23 to distinguish the paper's pre-Muon theoretical contribution from later optimizer engineering, scaling, and convergence results.
